utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Good morning, everybody. For the record, accused Beara is still sick, I presume. I start -- I don't see Mr. Ostojic, present, so Mr. Nikolic, I can barely see you behind the column. First, I would like to have a confirmation from you that a waiver is on its way, that there is no objection, that we proceed. And secondly, Mr. Ostojic had to inquire yesterday what happened to the waiver relating to the day before, or part of the sitting of the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know -- no, mine is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Beara did send his waiver since his health condition is still such that he cannot be present, and I believe that he sent a similar waiver for the previous day which I am going to check throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have an indication of how long this condition is going to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, no. He informed us that he was not feeling well, so we will monitor the situation during the day, and we will update the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much, Mr. Nikolic. For the record, today, Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution. And the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Ostojic for the time being. Good morning to you, Mr. Haynes, and good morning to you, Mr. Pandurevic. Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Pandurevic, I would simply like to implore you to slow down in your speaking so that the interpreters have a chance to interpret what you are saying. Yesterday afternoon, we finished with a document on the screen which was 7D1006, and I would just very briefly like to have it placed back on the screen so that we can conclude that area of the examination. Thank you. And just to remind you, I am sure you need no reminding, but we are talking about a report from the 1st of February, 1993, and combat action in Kamenica. And what I wanted to ask you is whether it was any part of your orders to cause the civilian population to move out of Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no such orders, but I have to say here that in the territory of Kamenica, at that time there was no civilian population residing in the villages closest to Zvornik. That is because in November 1992 there was fighting in that area, and only the Muslim armed forces could be found in that area. Some would further in-depth from Zvornik on the axis of our attack, there was civilian residing, and this report speaks about the procedure I applied. I offered the civilian population to freely leave the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the purpose of that was what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what, in fact, happened after the prisoner was returned to convey your message?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain number of civilians, villagers, that is, truth be told, did leave the area of combat activities. I don't have the exact information as to their exact number, but there were some of them. From some positions we were able to monitor their movements, and we know from our intelligence and the writings of the Muslim media that such things indeed did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can leave Kamenica now. And I want to just walk you through, fairly briefly, some of the significant combat actions you took part in in 1993. In April of 1993, was there an operation called Udar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that at Operation Proboj which was launched in January and ended sometime in mid-March 1993, by its scope and achievements was a very modest operation. And when we are talking about an operation for a soldier, this is a term that comprises widespread combat operations. We know that the American forces managed to occupy Iraq in a month. As for us, we managed to advance 15 kilometres over three months so that upon the completion of Operation Proboj towards the end of March and the beginning of April, we continued with Operation Udar from a different axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us just a little bit, please, about the scope and purpose of Operation Udar and the part you played in it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate directly in Operation Udar. This operation applied to the area covering the axis Skelani-Srebrenica. This is the direction from east to west, from the river Drina towards Skelani. Some parts of the units of the Zvornik Brigade under the command of Dragan Obrenovic did participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at about this time, in other words March and April of 1993, in your capacity as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, did you come into contact with the organs of the United Nations - and I am thinking in particular about UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The geographical position of Zvornik itself and the area where the Zvornik Brigade was deployed mandated contact and encounters with numerous international organisations of all kind. Our most frequent contacts were with UNPROFOR, i.e., the United Nations forces whose mandate was the establishment of peace and the separation of the warring parties in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an occasion and honour -- actually, I had several meetings with Mr. Morillon. I was surprised, pleasantly surprised, by his dedication to the mission at hand, by his objectivities, and by his charm. And it was a great honour for me to cooperate with the general of the great French army and the great French people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Morillon would pass quite often from Sarajevo en route to Belgrade via Zvornik. His roads would cross in the area of Zvornik, and our meetings started sometime towards the end of February and continued throughout March and April. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly when our first meeting took place; however, there were at least six or seven such meetings, and they took place either in my office or in the football ground where helicopters landed or somewhere else on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I will see if I can jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D1008, please, the regular combat report for the 5th of March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pandurevic, you might like to concentrate on the bottom half of paragraph 2, though, by all means read as much of the document as you need to.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does -- I think that's the first record we can find of your meeting him. Is that a meeting you recall? And perhaps you can explain the circumstances of it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says in this report that there was a meeting in the municipality of Zvornik, but before this meeting there was another meeting on the same day between Mr. Morillon and myself. General Morillon was on a mission, i.e., he was visiting the areas of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica, and his task was to meet the representatives of the Muslim authorities. In order for him to do that, my task was to provide the security of his passage across the separation line. South of the village of Drinjaca, some 20 kilometres from the town of Zvornik at the entrance to Konjevic Polje, there were minefields, and the road was blocked. We had to clear that on our side. The Muslims had to do it on their side, and the -- then Mr. Morillon could successfully cross. The agreement was for us to meet him in the same place on the following day on his way back. Again, to secure his safe passage back towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we could just take a brief look at 7D1115, a regular or daily combat report for the following day, the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Pandurevic, as is common in these reports, the events of the day seem to be recorded in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this report in paragraph 2, a references made to General Morillon. At that time, there were different pieces of information about the humanitarian situation in the areas of Cerska and Konjevic Polje. And one of the reasons why Mr. Morillon went there was to check that controversial information. Upon his return from that area and our meeting in Drinjaca, which took place very early in the morning, his APC pulled over, and we had breakfast together. We talked about the situation in Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and the general area of these two villages. He said that the situation was not as it was portrayed in the media. He said that the situation was rather difficult, very similar to the situation in all the other areas of Bosnia and that he was prepared to talk about all these things to the media. I asked him to join me in my vehicle and go to Zvornik municipality where he would talk to the media. He did that, and I believe that after that press conference he was exposed to fierce attacks and criticism on the part of the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to show that these things are reported from both sides, can we have a look at 7D752. And this is a UN headquarters Bosnia and Herzegovina command Sarajevo report. And we'll start by looking at paragraph 1 on page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which reads in the English: "General Morillon and a team of representatives from various humanitarian agencies visited the villages of Cerska and Konjevic Polje on the 5th and 6th of March in order to assess the real situation in the area and to identify what humanitarian assistance was actually required."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then can we have a look at page 5 in the document, paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which reads: "It was alleged and supported by a Reuters journalist that the Serbs had been putting strong attacks Sase and Potocari, a Messerschmitt of world war two village had been shot down in January; the wreckage was in the Potocari region. He also stated that he seen single crop sprayers dropping bombs on Srebrenica, that this had stopped about a month ago. It was believed that the air transcript strip they flew from was at the eastern end of Bratunac. The Serb commander in Zvornik, Colonel Andric confirmed this, stating that there had been three of them but that the aircraft were no longer serviceable." The reference to Colonel Andric, do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be a thing that either the name was mixed up or the commander of the defence of Sekovici. Given the contents of this, I didn't know that the aircraft of this type were used at that time in that area. I knew sometime in June or July that some sort of improvised landing strip was organised in the area of Bratunac and that some farming aircraft were used or there were attempts to use them, but that did not work out. In what area or on what facilities, I really wouldn't be able to tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall having any such conversation with General Morillon or anybody from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, although we did talk. I could not provide him with any information of any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can we move on then, please, to the 11th of March, and can we see 7D948. And this is a collection of regular combat reports, and we need to start with page 2 in the B/C/S, and in the English pages 3 and 4. I am at it again, it should say 7D948 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to confound me, Mr. Pandurevic, this time an event of the day appears in paragraph 4 rather than paragraph 2 of the report. Is this a visit that you recall? And can you amplify it in terms of any meeting or discussion that you had.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that Mr. Morillon visited the wounded at the medical centre in Zvornik. However, I don't recall any details relating to this visit. It must have been a routine visit en route to Srebrenica and, therefore, I am not able to provide any further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on then, please, to page 5 in the B/C/S, and in the English pages 9 and 10. A daily combat report for the 8th of April, 1993. And here it's paragraph 5 beginning at around 11 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "General Morillon on his way to Srebrenica entered into the city of Zvornik; however, at the very entrance of the city, he was stopped by hundred women and children who did not allow him to continue his journey towards Srebrenica. The reasons for their actions were the unfilled promises from the earlier agreement in relation to the Serbs in Tuzla upon insistent cities residents impeded General Morillon to return from Zvornik, to make his way to Tuzla rather than towards the SRJ and the bridges towards the Drina river." What's that all about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were negotiations in progress at the time about evacuation of the Serbian population from the Tuzla area and the town itself. Mr. Morillon was involved in that process. At the same time, he was trying to arrange evacuation of population from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Since no Serbian convoy left Tuzla, a large number of civilians and their relatives living in Zvornik were apparently dissatisfied with such a development, and they assembled in order to prevent the passage of Mr. Morillon and his escort towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved having learned about this incident, I tried to persuade the population to disperse and to open up the road and enable Mr. Morillon to carry on. It took quite a lot of time. These negotiations and attempts at persuasion were difficult. Mr. Morillon was sitting in his APC, and the crowd around started to act like a mob. And, normally, in such circumstances you cannot have properly articulated requests or any reasonable conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just have a look at 7D1030.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Some photographs of you as a much younger man, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can probably just flip through them, there are only three or four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are these photographs from the 8th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that these photographs are related to the events that I spoke about. I suppose that's the date. I was personally there next to the APC of General Morillon along with a number of policemen, and the only thing that I was able to do was to protect the General, himself; however, I failed to persuade the civilians to disperse in order to allow him to continue his journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And whilst we are looking at paragraphs, can we have a look at 7D937, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, is that a photograph taken on the same occasion when General Morillon was impeded by the civilian population or on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken on another occasion when Mr. Morillon was visiting me in my office, and we had this photograph taken after we finished the meeting. It was taken with his camera. And after a while, when he came again, he gave me this photograph when he alighted from a helicopter on a football pitch, and he also put his signature on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just two or three more questions on this particular area. And people seem to have made a habit of impeding General Morillon's presence one way or another. When his presence was impeded in Zvornik on the 8th of April, did you have anything to do with the organisation of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. My task was to enable free movement of Mr. Morillon in carrying out his duties and mission while moving through the area, that was my responsibility. In this particular situation, I reported to the Main Staff and corps command, and General Milovanovic arrived in a helicopter and became personally involved in trying to resolve this problem. And after that, Mr. Morillon returned towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On a more general level, throughout the months of March and April when you were dealing with him, what was your attitude to him and any requests he made of you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, at the beginning Mr. Morillon was carrying out his duties really professionally with dignity and commitment. At the time, as a major, I was honoured to maintain contacts with a high-ranking general. His requests posed to me as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade were for me to ensure free movement and free passage while he was carrying out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you comply with those requests?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Anyway, there was an order from the Main Staff and the Drina Corps to ensure that all the UNPROFOR forces can carry out their tasks unimpedingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On a personal level, what was your attitude to the presence of UNPROFOR in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR passed most often through the area where I was. They didn't carry out any significant missions in the area of Zvornik; therefore, I am not able to give you any specific assessment of the quality of what they did apart from my contacts with Mr. Morillon. I think that at the time UNPROFOR was involved in carrying out missions to the best of their ability. Later on, they took a different approach, and more and more reports were coming about biased conduct of UNPROFOR throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll just move a little out of sequence because it's a linked topic. As we know, convoys of food stuffs and other humanitarian aid from time to time passed through Zvornik. What role did you personally play in the policing of convoys?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the Zvornik Brigade was part of the general role of the VRS in terms of the convoys passing through the area. Since this was a border crossing, and convoys often came from Belgrade, and pursuant to the orders received from superior commands and the usual procedure, the contents of these convoys were examined in accordance with the documents that they were carried with them. As the commander, I was not directly involved in these procedures because I entrusted a reserve captain who was a former bank manager and who was skilled to do this task to carry out these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What authorisation did the brigade have to allow or deny the passage of a convoy?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade didn't have any powers to either allow or reject the passage of convoys. The people who manned check-points were only to act in compliance with the usual procedure upon receiving a notice that a convoy was coming and to check the contents of what they are carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, how many convoys were stopped by the Zvornik Brigade under the authority of the former bank manager who, I think his name is Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the convoys were stopped there and checked. If everything tallied with the declaration that the convoy leader had on him, they would be allowed to continue. However, if certain commodities or other items were detected that were not permissible to be transported in that way, then the superior command would be advised, and they would tell us what to do in that situation. I remember two instances when in two convoys certain items were found that were not intended for humanitarian purposes and could have been used for military purposes. And I think that there are also video reports and other reports about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to finish with that topic. So far as you were aware, did you receive any order to deliberately obstruct convoys of aid in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any order for us to deliberately obstruct the passage of any convoys on our own initiative. As far as I can remember, they passed smoothly because they were headed for Tuzla and Sarajevo and Srebrenica as well, and it was a very intense traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a combat mission, and it took up a lot of our time. It only just created problems for us rather than facilitating the situation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, stepping back into our, as it were, brief history of combat operations in 1993, in May of 1993 there was - if everybody will forgive me for leading you on this - a referendum on the Vance-Owen Plan. How, firstly, did that impact upon your job?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, can we get his understanding of what the -- that was, so we'll get an understanding of the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You interrupted my thought process. I was thinking about asking that question first rather than second. I don't care in which way the questions are answered. It's a sensible interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did the Vance-Owen Plan mean to you in practical terms, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, and I believe as for every other soldier, any attempt at restoring peace and putting an end to a war would be the best news ever that could be heard and would be a great relief. No soldier wants to fight a war. Therefore, we anticipated that the Vance-Owen Plan would offer an opportunity to satisfy the interests of all parties involved in the conflict and that peace would ensue. At the moment I cannot recall the details of the plan, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What practically did it mean you had to do in the month of May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean referring to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, a referendum was called in order to have this plan accepted. And since all citizens who had a voting right were supposed to take part in the referendum, I remember that command organs were to be involved in the voting at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Can we move on then, please, to June of 1993 and something about which we've heard a fair bit of evidence already. Operation Mac 1. Can you tell us a little bit about the purpose of that operation and your involvement in it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Mac 1 was planned at the level of the Main Staff of the VRS. During this trial we had an opportunity to see these documents, and, of course, the Drina Corps was to spear-head this action. And, from the Zvornik Brigade, a combat group equalling a battalion was also involved which was based on the Podrinje regiment. The task was to operate along the Rogatica-Ustipraca axis and to reach the left bank of the river Drina in the area where the villages of Medjedja and Ustipraca were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As I say, we've heard a little about it. How many battle or combat groups were involved in the operation other than your own?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation was conducted in the general area. Some of the forces were acted from the direction of Visegrad, some from Rudo and Cajnice, and the forces under my command including elements of the Rogatica Brigade and the 2nd Romanija Brigade -- Motorised Brigade, which means that all the activities took place in the general area of upper Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What particular task did your combat group have?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My combat group had a task to reach Ustipraca and thereby cut off the retreat route for the forces that were deployed north of Ustipraca towards Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how successful were you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were relatively successful. In a relatively short period of time, we managed to reach the Ustipraca sector and to cut off the Visegrad-Gorazde road in the area of Ustipraca. That section of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Haynes, please. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am sorry to interrupt. I would just like to have a bit of a clarification. Maybe it's a translation issue. In English, the terms "combat group," "battle group," and "tactical group," have very different meanings. Maybe when they are translated to general they take the same meaning. I would just like if you could clarify this, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Haynes, would you take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Pandurevic, what was the unit you were in command of? Was it a battle group, a command group, or a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will first try to explain what a tactical group means. A tactical group is a provisional formation set up of a number of combat groups for the purpose of executing a specific task within a certain period of time and in a certain place. The size of a tactical group is usually equivalent to that of a battalion, but it has reinforcements. These reinforcements can be either artillery reinforcements or armoured and mechanized forces. A combat group can be part of the tactical group, therefore, it's smaller in size and strength, but it sometimes can be almost identical to a tactical group. Therefore, the combat group under my command in Operation Mac 1, in its strength and size, was almost the same as a tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in comparison to you, what degree of success did the other units have in that operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to assess the success of other units involved in this operation would be best made by the person who was commanding all the forces taking part in the operation. I could only evaluate how my adjacent units on the left and the right performed. The unit on my left were made of elements of the Visegrad Brigade, and their axis of attack was much more difficult, and their success dependent on my success. Therefore, the operation of my forces on the flank enabled them to carry out their mission better. The forces acting on the right bank of the river Drina, I believe that at the time were the least successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we know the answer to this, I think, but who was in command of the operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic commanded the operation from the forward command post in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the command --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the commander of the forces to the left and the commander of the forces on the right bank of the Drina were who?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander on the right - or, actually, this was a unit made up of elements of Rogatica Brigade - were not actually involved in direct combat. They were just securing my right flank. And the left forces were under the command of Colonel Luka Dragicevic of the Visegrad Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what was the significance of your reaching the Ustipraca section?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In combat there is always an attempt to use the least effort and least use of potential to accomplish a task. One tries to find the weakest point on the enemy's side, and in this case this was cutting off his withdrawal route and bringing their forces into an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, in combat that might be what you always try to do, but is that what you had done by reaching the Ustipraca section?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the enemy forces at Ustipraca?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Muslim forces in the area of Medjedja and Ustipraca was Mr. Sejdic, Ahmed by name. I talked to him over the radio, and I had a previous communication with him and organised several exchanges of both dead and -- dead bodies and prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you'd cut his forces off, what was their position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His forces were along the Drina river in the territory of Medjedja village, and their position was absolutely inferior with regard to the forces that were under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you spoke to him, what did you speak about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our communications means could easily be intercepted, and we knew each other's voices. His signalsman knew my voice, and vice versa. He used my code-name Granicar, and I used to call him by his code-name, Captain. His signalsman said, "Granicar, We know that you are there, come in, please." I responded, and I wanted to be put through to Mr. Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am not sure it's clear from your answer; did he call you, or did you call him first?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His signalsman recognized my voice. He came in, and he said that he was aware of my presence on the line and asked for me to come in, which I did, and asked him to put me through to Mr. Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am sorry, that was probably clear. It's probably my fault. And when did you speak to him, what was the topic of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first words we exchanged were greetings. We talked about our previous experiences and activities, and then we started talking about a current tactical situation that his forces was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he propose or did you suggest?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him if he saw how far my forces had reached and whether he knew the exact deployment of my forces. He said that he knew that we had reached Ustipraca and that he was cut off. My proposal to him was to tell everybody in the area of Medjedja to take the road freely, either in vehicles or on foot, and that they can proceed in the direction of Gorazde. I guaranteed him that my soldiers would not open fire, that they would not fire a single bullet in their direction. He listened to my proposal. He hesitated a little. He asked me to corroborate my guarantee in one way or another. And I then told him that it would be his choice whether he would be leading the column or whether he would be at its rear, that it was up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, Well, if that is the case, I'll be in a blue Mercedes at the very back of the column. I said, Yes, you have my guarantee, you can proceed freely. And then what we had agreed was later on honoured and everything happened as it had been agreed between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did the evacuation of this column take place after the conversation you had?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the talks started sometime early in the afternoon and lasted until dusk of the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when did the column leave?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time that I have just indicated, both the civilians and the soldiers went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you estimate for us how many people you let go?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to be precise about the number of people. I can only give you the estimate of how many there had been there before that, and I can say that at least 3.000 or 4.000 people were evacuated on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about military hardware?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the soldiers and military hardware that the Muslims had was able to leave the area. I was familiar with some of their vehicles that they used for the exchanges of the fallen soldiers in November 1992, and I saw the same vehicles on the day of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what authority did you have to enter into this agreement with Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any authority whatsoever, nor did I ever ask for it. In that specific situation, I acted the best I saw fit. My task was to reach Ustipraca, and I accomplished that mission successfully. I reported back the my command and gave them the position of my units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So why did you reach and honour this agreement with Mr. Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason is very simple, there was no point in engaging in further combat and exposing those who should not have been at risk to further risk. I had accomplished my combat mission, and it was not in my interest to inflict damage or victimise people on any of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think you may I have already told us a goodly portion of this, but in the second part of June of 1993, there was another operation called Sword or Mac planned, Mac 2. What happened to that operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, Sword 1 should have been continued. There should not have been interruptions between the two. However, due to bad coordination between the units, the operation was interrupted and some of the units withdrew from that area. Among those units were also the units of the Zvornik Brigade. Only a few days later were the groups brought back and combat continued from the direction of Cajnice and Gorazde, and then that operation got the name Sword 2 or Mac 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, it's past 10.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was planning to go to 10.20, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you play a part in Mac 2?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally I was not supposed to. Later on I joined and I participated in the combat, but that lasted a bit shorter than Operation Sword 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the thrust of that operation? And what did you achieve, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, the goal was to repel the Muslim forces further away from Cajnice, and to reclaim the Serbian villages on the right bank of the Drina in the sector of Gorazde and to take the features from which Cajnice could be successfully defended. Our success there was limited. The operation was halted there. And as far as I can remember, there were no further actions on that axis in the course of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There was a further action in July of 1993 called Lukavac. Did units of the Zvornik Brigade take part in that? And did you personally take part in that? And where was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Lukavac 1993 was an operation that had been planned and carried out by the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska in my understanding, at least. And it was carried out in the territory of Trnovo and Sarajevo and Bjelasnica mountain. Elements of the Zvornik Brigade units on the strength of the Drina Corps participated in that operation; however, I myself did not participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I just briefly want to take us into 1994. In April to July of 1994 was there an operation called - I am never going to pronounce this correctly - Zvijezda?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Operation Zvijezda, and under that name, was carried out in the general area between Rogatica and Gorazde. There was an attempt to take a mountain pass between Rogatica and Gorazde. One unit of the Zvornik Brigade did participate in that, and I remember that the young second lieutenant was killed. He had just joined fresh from the academy. I can't give you the exact dates of any of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Other than that, was there any significant combat activity throughout the whole period from the summer of 1993 until the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Zvornik, there were no significant combat activities. However, units and elements of the Zvornik Brigade were involved partly in defence activities and active activities outside of their zone; partly in the zone of the Drina Corps and partly in the zone of the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps. Towards the end of 1994, in the area of Zvornik on the north western part of the front line, in the direction of Teocak, there were some combat actions with a view to repairing the tactical position. However, due to bad weather conditions and snow almost no significant results were achieved as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what were you principally engaged in during that period of time from July 1993 until the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged in my duties as a brigade commander. I sent the forces outside of the brigade zone of activity. I toured the brigade. I controlled the situation in the units, that's at least what we call this in the military. I was engaged in daily command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in terms of the units, you gave us on Tuesday of this week a description of the personnel that made up your battalions. Did they change greatly from December 1992 until the end of 1994, or were they the same people?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A battalion is a tactical unit with permanent composition. When I say that they have "permanent composition," that means that they have strictly defined units which are companies, support units, and logistics units. The number of companies within the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade varied. It was not in keeping with the establishment rules. As far as their position is concerned and as far as the defence sectors are concerned, from 1993 until the very end of the war, they were more or less identical, which means that they kept almost identical position throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I really meant the people in the battalions, were they the same people?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the people were the same, and they hailed from the same area, still. Some got killed, some got wounded, but we did not have any special sources of replenishment, no other areas from which our men would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be it for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's briefly, together, Mr. Pandurevic, have a look at P5, Supreme Command Directive 7 dated the 8th of March 1995. We are not going to look at this for very long. When did you first see Directive 7, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it here in The Hague when I was shown all the documents on the EDS system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's look at, as it were, it's the subsequent document to that, which is P203. And this is the order of the Drina Corps of the 20th of March headed "The Order for Defence and Active Combat Operations Operative number 7." As the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, it's addressed to you. Did you in the spring of 1995 receive it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a -- the "Order for Defence and Activity Combat Operations, Operative Number 7." It was sent to all the brigades, i.e., subordinated units of the Drina Corps, which also included Zvornik Brigade. And, yes, I did receive this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could turn to page 5 in the document and page 9 in the English. And paragraph 5.1, the tasks of the unit, the 1st Zvornik Brigade -- 1st Zvornik infantry brigade: "With persistent and active defence of the assigned area of responsibility in cooperation with the 1st Bratunac Brigade available forces from the Zvornik MUP and a unit of conscripts on work obligation has the obligation has the following tasks: To prevent the enemy breakthrough along the selected tactical axis, taking control of the dominant features, cutting the Zvornik-Kozluk road, and reaching the Drina river. With diverse reactive combat operations using operational and tactical camouflage measures tie as many enemy forces as possible during the execution of the operation carried out by the Bosnia corps and the Drina corps and inflict the greatest possible losses, personal and material, and with your own forces plan the execution of combat operations in order to improve tactical position in your own area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, now, wait until the interpreter -- I know that they have the text in B/C/S, but they still have to catch up with you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am very, very sorry to the interpreters. "The brigade command shall form --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, because I just want to make sure that they have cute up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's a schoolboy error. I should be watching the transcript. All right. Let's proceed. "The brigade command shall form battalion-strength ready forces for the intervention along threatened axis and carrying out offensive operations in their area of responsibility and by order of the Drina Corps commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have now, and I read it quite a along time ago as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you read it upon first receipt, did you understand the Zvornik Brigade to have any task relating to Srebrenica or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task assigned here to the Zvornik Brigade and the way it is worded may be considered as an ongoing task which the brigade was supposed to carry out throughout the war, and the task is decisive defence of the assigned area; i.e., to stop the enemy from reaching the Drina river and interrupting the road Zvornik-Kozluk-Bijeljina. This was my principal task, always, and it remained so until the end of the war. The second part of this task, i.e., to improve tactical position in the area of responsibility is something that we carried out throughout the war. And this part where we were supposed to form battalion strength ready forces, we did have those forces and we even reinforced them. We knew that we could always be used in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps and outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This order was dated the 20th of March of 1995, what operations did the Zvornik Brigade actually carry out in pursuance of it within the next three months?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this order was subsequently enlarged by combat orders which carried to -- followed in the realisation of the Spreca 95 operation, the one that has been discussed at great length here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we need to look at the tasks of the corps as described by this document, and they are set out at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which is page 5 and 6 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. So we need to turn to that, please, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I think rather than have me read into the transcript a section which runs over three pages, would you just read through that section to yourself, Mr. Pandurevic. And when you're done, would you let me know.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And bearing that in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 8 in the English, which I think will be page 4 in the B/C/S. It is page 4 in B/C/S. And that says: "I have decided with persistent and active defence of the frontlines from Orica Vis at the right boarder of the area of responsibility to Gradina at the left board of the corps area of responsibility and around the enclaved in Podrinje in cooperation with the elements of the SRK forces, prevent an enemy breakthrough along the selected operative tactical axes with main forces and tie down as many enemy troops as possible through diversionary actions and operative tactical camouflage measures, separate physically the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and prevent any communications between the enclaves, and with auxiliary forces (the forces in readiness) carry out the Spreca 95 operation in cooperation with the IBK forces, the objective to cut the Muslim forces along the Kalesija-Simin Han line and then breakup and destroy the enemy forces in the area of Teocak, Sapna, and Vitinica, thus finally removing the danger of a Muslim breakthrough towards the Drina north of Zvornik. "During the execution of Zvijezda 95 operation and in cooperation with SRK and HK forces, liberate the areas of the Gorazde enclave and reduce the enclave to the size of the protected area of 3 kilometres from the town centre. And in case UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, execute the operation named Jadar, then breakup and destroy the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberate the Drina ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's not beat about the bush. The first half of the section headed "Tasks of the Drina Corps" replicates Directive 7, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2, the tasks of the Drina Corps, was copied, literally, from Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After the paragraph which related directly to your unit, the Zvornik Brigade, what was the most important area of this report -- of this order, sorry?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the task assigned to the Zvornik Brigade was of such nature that it had to do exclusively with the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, provided that it had one battalion stand by for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were the tasks of the Drina Corps important for you to note and understand?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task assigned to the Drina Corps was a very complex and complicated one. It was not limited in terms of time, whether it should -- when it should commence and when it should end. But, Your Honours, since I have seen with how much attention you look through the documents, to give me some more time to explain to you how this document prepared by the command of the Drina Corps came about to be drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Directive 7, as we saw, was addressed to the corps. Corps commanders were obliged to literally re-write the task assigned to corps from the directive. They must not change a single letter. For that reason, General Zivanovic formulated the task in a manner that he did. What is important, however, in this order issued by the Drina Corps command, and that is from item 4 onwards, which begins "I have decided ..." And this is his idea underlying the decision which he's presenting there with a view how to implement the tasks that he has received. His basic idea, which is a part of the decision, has applied a slightly different form and slightly different meaning when defining the activities of the Drina Corps. The corps tasks stem from the basic idea, and we can see that there is a link between the idea underlying the decision, which is item 4, and the tasks assigned to the Drina Corps brigades. For that reason, some part of the assigned -- assignments given to the Drina Corps based on Directive 7 are not incorporated in the task of brigade nor in the basic idea of the corps command, and that is this infamous sentence that has been mentioned here on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why would that be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander issues a decision. Once he -- he's done that, his superior officer has to approve it, in this case this is the commander of the Main Staff. When I received a decision from the corps command, I am interested to hear the underlying part, which is item 4, and on the other hand what the tasks of my brigade and the adjacent units are and nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you think that your orders under this document included a task to remove the civilian population from Srebrenica or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task given to the Zvornik Brigade has nothing to do with the area of either Srebrenica or Zepa and, hence, with the population in those two enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And looking at the order of the corps commander, did you form the opinion that that objective was part of the corps' plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objective, leading. We are now getting into substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is leading Mr. -- I don't think I need to consult my colleagues on this. On the other hand, is it so critical?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would really like to hear the General's opinion, not his agreement or disagreement with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on these issues it is, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And sorry for overlapping. Can you rephrase it please, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you see as the corps' objectives in relation to Srebrenica and Zepa under this order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for me to comprehend this at all, I had to take the following approach: Each command including a brigade command when they receive an order, like this one that we see in front of us, we study the task contained therein. One of the stages of studying the task involves studying it and trying to comprehend and understand the idea and the objective of my commander, what he wants to achieve and in what way he wants to achieve. And, also, which forces he would want to use them and what kind of maneuver action he wants to undertake. Therefore, I understood item 4 in a way that my corps commander wants to put up a persistent and decisive defence and thereby prevent communications between -- Srebrenica and Zepa enclave and to take part in the planning and execution of joint operations. From his idea I could not draw any conclusion that his task was to evacuate the population from these enclaves and to annihilate them all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, going back to, as it were, the infamous words which are set out under paragraph 2, the tasks of the Drina Corps, how did you or do you view the tasks of the Drina Corps under that heading in terms of achievability?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received this order, I first read it, and we call it the first reading, just to get the general idea. During that first reading I noticed item 2, the task of the corps; however, I didn't dwell long on it. And during the next reading and analysing, I focused on item 4. I cannot tell you now exactly what I understood at the time, the sentence that has been mentioned here, but definitely I gave it a lot of thought during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You're probably one question ahead of me, in fact. What I was asking you was the general list of tasks for the Drina Corps under Directive 7, what view did you have as to the scope and achievability of those tasks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't see this on the screen, but I know what tasks we are talking about. It's a whole series of tasks that cannot be executed within a short period of time. It's a series of tasks relating to completely different areas. These are tasks that have to be carried out either by the Drina Corps itself or in a concerted action with other corps. So it involves a number of tasks that have to be carried out along -- in a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as to the phrase "create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life," how did you or do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get the whole phrase in the record. I think that's going to be an important part of his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mind. It might be best if we answer the General's complaint and have that paragraph put back on the screen in front of him. So if we can go back to, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Page 6. I don't see it in B/C/S yet. It should be paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wrong B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have to move one further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes? I would really like to thank Mr. McCloskey, because I also wanted to see this full sentence. But first of all, I would like to say that the very word "enclave," and "Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves," have a meaning of their own. They were isolated and became enclaves thanks to the front-line of the 28th Division. By way of its combat deployment, the 28th Division encircled its own population and thereby created an enclave. Now, what it says here, "By planned and well thought-out combat operations ..." It doesn't say which. There are all kinds of combat activities that this task can be achieved with. Given that the population lived in the enclave in the way that they did because the enclave had not been demilitarised and that it was necessary to remove the 28th Division as a military threat from that area, it seems that the author of this document thought that this population was exposed from propaganda and other activities from outside, can be incited and turned against their own leaders. We know that in Srebrenica there were two faction: One that advocated combat at any cost and the other one which wanted total disarmament and life in peace. We experienced a similar experience during the NATO aggression and bombing of certain facilities in Serbia, the aim of which was topple the regime of Slobodan Milosevic by engaging the insider forces. This is how I read this document had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, is that what you thought when you first read it? Or is that the thoughts you had having considered it years later?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that during the first reading of this order, I didn't take -- pay too much attention to it. I didn't memorize it, and I did not think about it in the way I think about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to clarify how you've come to interpret it, what facilities were you talking about in Serbia that were bombed by NATO planes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were non-military facilities; for example, electric grid, bridges, roads, railroads, everything that can make life for the civilian population hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why was that done?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wesley Clark and Slobodan Milosevic knew that better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to leave that document and turn to a rather different document about a month later in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look please at P2920.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go straight to page 3 in both languages so that you can confirm for us that this is a document with your signature on it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a document that came out of the Zvornik Brigade, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page, now. We can see it's dated the 25th of April, and it says "Report number 88."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information addressed, as you can see here, to the Drina Corps, one copy, and probably other copies were forwarded to subordinate units of the Zvornik Brigade. This document was produced by the organ for morale, religious, and legal affairs. And the purpose is to inform the units, our own units, about the psychological and propaganda activities aimed at the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know the person who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was written by Major Nenad Simic, assistant for moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what does it mean that it says "Report number 88"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably means that this is a sequential number, or it is a document number 88 from his remit or from his scope of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did that organ write many reports?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, just like all other organs who wrote various documents relating to their area of responsibility and scope of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, other than writing reports like this -- well, I don't know they are all like this. But other than writing reports, what did Mr. Nenad Simic's job entail?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to writing these reports, Mr. Nenad Simic was involved in arranging funerals for the fighters who were killed, providing for their families, supplying humanitarian aid, and things of the similar nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what had been happening to him about the 25th of April 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he did not live in Zvornik. He was living somewhere in Central Bosnia in a village near Zivinice, as far as I remember. And at the beginning of the war, he had experienced a personal tragedy when his son was killed. That is why he arranged these funerals, and he attended the funerals of the fallen fighters, and he expressed condolences to the families that were affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you read this before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just glanced at it without reading the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when it was produced in this court a year or so ago and you read it, what was your reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reaction was the same both then and now. It should never have been written, and my signature should never have been put on this kind of document because there are certain parts and sections that, as they are, should never have been included in this kind of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to satisfy all our curiosity, do you know the derivation of the word "poturice"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot has been said about this word and other words as well. I don't like to go back into history, especially not too far back into history, and for that I apologise to this Court. But I will have to say a few sentences about this. The word "poturica" originates from the 15th century which is the time when the Ottoman empire occupied the Balkans. This word contained religious and cultural features and connotations. It is related to a specific period in time, to a specific empire, and to the culture that grew as a result of the rule of that empire. This word, "poturice" was used both in Bosnia and in other Balkan countries and it became rather prominent in the last war. It did not, however, have any specific meaning, but it would have been better if it didn't have the meaning that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I won't lead you. Is it a nice thing to say to somebody?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the term is nice if you use it for somebody. But I know from practice that Muslims also use this word in addressing each other, and they don't think much of it. Serbs also call themselves Chetniks, and they don't think much of it. However, if the word is used between the two different ethnic groups, it assumes a different connotation. There is a Muslim family named "Poturak" which also originates from that word "poturice," just by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Haynes, but what does it actually mean? Literally translated, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think General Pandurevic can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the process of Islamisation, which is a process that which taking place in the Balkans when Christians were converted into Islam, since this was done by the Turkish, authorities which represented the Islam in the Balkans at the time, whoever was converted into Islam somehow was perceived as being on the side of the Turks. But they were not referred to as Turks, but "poturice," the convert. Or they would also call them Crypto-Christians which means covert-Christians. This is as much as I know about the history of this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sure we are all very grateful. Be the use of such terms -- I'm sorry, I am going to start this again. Were such words always used in documents of the brigade during the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not used throughout the war -- or, rather, from its beginning. At one point in the war, they creeped into our documents. I don't know exactly what that happened. You can see in the documents themselves. In any case, it was in 1992 and the forward or most part of 1993 when the word "enemy" was used. I even found some reports dating back to November 1992 where it -- where in one of the reports it says "The blue." And that was the word that was used in the staff military games in peacetime. The enemy was always represented as "blue," and our own forces were red, and that was the colours that we used on our combat maps. Six months into the war, some people were still not aware of the reality of the situation. They were not aware that the war was really going on, but as the war continued, as the casualties mounted, the anger and hatred also mounted, and those words assumed a different meaning and gained in prominence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this topic for too long, but just way of illustration --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we take a look at 7D965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a quick question, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All the other reports coming from Zvornik Infantry Brigade has the title either "regular combat report" or either "interim combat report." This document says just "report." Does it have any connotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? Your Honours, this is about two different types of documents. Regular and interim combat reports are documents that are drafted daily, on a daily basis. And this is information that is tied to a different organ in the brigade command, the organ for morale, religious, and political affairs. This information was drafted periodically. That's why it is not entitled "Report" but rather "Information" in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to conclude this topic we are going to have a look at a document from 1992. It's a Main Staff document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And people are free to read through it, but as you observed, Mr. Pandurevic, it begins: "The enemy are taking advantage of various talks regarding peace and truce and are trying to use their last chance to attain some positions in the battle-field of in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. "This refers in particular to Muslims ..." And two paragraphs lower it refers to the Muslims enemy, and people can read through it. You've read a lot of documents, and it's your observation, is it, that at the start of the war such terms were not used in army documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already answered --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that question. And if I may ask him again on going back to "poturice," I have something here which tells me that "poturice" is a degenerate or hypocrite. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not how I interpreted the word or how I perceived it, for that matter. However, those who were converted into Islam did not do it of their own will. Some did, but some were under pressure, and they were forced to be converted. There were cases, for example, of one brother remaining Christian and the other becoming Muslim, so the Muslim brother would put pressure on the Christian brother to convert. Maybe, between the two of them, there were such an understanding of this word. However, Your Honour, I have never tied such connotations to this word. I've never been aware of -- of this connotation, and I am sure that it cannot be applied to a whole group of people or even a whole ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, in fact, a rather better document to illustrate your own point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One that you signed, 7D946, from January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we need to see page 5 in the B/C/S and page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you identify that as your regular combat report from the date of the 9th of January 1993? We can all read the words.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the night, the enemy did not carry out any major offensive activities except for minor provocations ..." et cetera, "However, a large concentration of enemy forces was observed in the sector of the village of Jajici," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the word that is used here is "the enemy" and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. In May and June of 1995, were both you and Dragan Obrenovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you continue, I stand to be corrected, but I want to make sure. If you go to page 40, line 9, 8 and 9: "To conclude on this topic, we are going to have a look at the document from 1992 ..." And then you ask questions, I pointed out he has already answered, et cetera. But we don't have a record of the -- of the reference of that document, because then you move to another two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was 7D945, and then 7D946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 946 we have, but we don't have 945. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the question I was in the course of asking you was, in May and June of 1995 were both you and Dragan Obrenovic present in your offices at the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not present together. Major Dragan Obrenovic had been wounded in mid-April during Spreca 95 operation, and he was being either -- he was in treatment, and I was on my own at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the month of June, were the forces of the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Wolves entirely located within the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some troops of the Drina Wolves were in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, and some of them were carrying out a task in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first find out about Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this was on the 1st July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did you first find out?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic called all the brigade commanders -- actually, not all of us, some of us, and I don't know exactly where we met, but in any case we went to Pribicevac where we carried out commanding, reconnoitering that had to with Krivaja 95 Operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would like just quickly to look at 5D351, please. And if I can -- this is a regular combat report of the 20th of June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to paragraph 2, and in particular the entry, "as of today, 955 soldiers are engaged outside the brigade's zone of responsibility." And it then lists where the various of them are. Given that sort of commitment to other theatres of war at that time, would you have anticipated for -- that the brigade would be asked to form another battalion to go outside its area of defence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of this regular combat report and its contents was to be used as information for the corps command when they considered possible engagement of the Zvornik Brigade. They were supposed to know exactly what resources that the Zvornik Brigade had at its disposal in its own area of responsibility and which of them are outside of their area of responsibility. I, as a commander, did not expect that -- that I would be asked by anybody to put the Zvornik Brigade under even more pressure and to extend its resources even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did General Krstic tell you about the proposed operation on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the group that was engaged in the commander's reconnaissance spent some time in Milici and had lunch there. I don't know whether this preceded the reconnaissance of followed it, I don't know. But I know that we visited three working points from which we carried out commander's reconnaissance and estimated possible directions of use of the Drina Corps. And during that reconnaissance, General Krstic told us that -- that the enclaves had to be separate completely, that communication had to be interrupted between Zepa and Srebrenica, and that the 28th Division should be prevented from moving on towards the Sarajevo theater of war where the Muslim forces, either BiH Army attempted to carry out the lifting of the blockade, and they wanted to launch a strategic operation aimed at reaching the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you know during the course of that meeting what the commitment of your brigade was to be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a point immediately below Pribicevac, which commands the best view of the planned direction of the use of the forces from my brigade, I was given the exact direction and targets, i.e., the exact way I was going to use the units and the lines I was supposed to reach as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in terms of the planning of a military operation, was there anything unusual about the processes that lead up to Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to planning at the operational level, such as the level of corps, I don't know of any such situation happening before, i.e., that on the same day commander's reconnaissance would be carried out, a decision would be taken, and the following day the use of troops would be ordered. Reconnaissance one day before use or -- this can be done only at the level of battalion or company, at a tactical level, that is. In other words, this decision on active combat operations dubbed Krivaja 95 was an ad hoc operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you were told of the purpose of the operation, what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
